content: Infant mortality refers to the death of an infant before reaching their first birthday. The infant mortality rate is a critical indicator of the overall health and well-being of a society. In 2021, the infant mortality rate in the United States was 5.4 deaths per 1,000 live births. In 2021, nearly 20,000 infants died in the United States. The five leading causes of infant mortality during that year were: 1. Birth defects. 2. Preterm birth and low birth weight. 3. Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS). 4. Injuries, such as suffocation. 5. Complications related to maternal pregnancy. In 2021, 19 states achieved the Healthy People 2030 target of 5.0 or fewer infant deaths per 1,000 live births. Healthy People 2030 is a set of science-based, 10-year national objectives aimed at improving the health of all Americans. Geographically, the highest infant mortality rates in 2021 were observed in states located in the South, Alaska, and the Midwest. Infant mortality rates in 2021 varied significantly by race and ethnicity: Non-Hispanic Black infants had the highest mortality rate at 10.6 deaths per 1,000 live births. Non-Hispanic Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander infants had a rate of 7.8. Non-Hispanic American Indian/Alaska Native infants had a rate of 7.5. Hispanic infants had a rate of 4.8. Non-Hispanic White infants had a rate of 4.4. Non-Hispanic Asian infants had the lowest rate at 3.7. The CDC is actively working to improve infant health outcomes by collaborating with healthcare providers, public health agencies, communities, and other partners. This collaborative approach aims to address the social, behavioral, and health-related risk factors that contribute to infant mortality. The CDC supports 36 Perinatal Quality Collaboratives (PQCs), which are state or multistate networks of multidisciplinary teams focused on improving the quality of care for mothers and infants. The Maternal and Child Health Epidemiology Program (MCHEP) assigns epidemiologists and fellows to states, localities, and tribal areas. These experts conduct research and provide scientific data to enhance maternal and child health programs and policies. To better understand and address sudden unexpected infant death (SUID), the CDC supports the SUID and Sudden Death in the Young (SDY) Case Registry in 32 sites. These sites collect and analyze data on SUID trends and circumstances to develop strategies aimed at reducing future deaths. The Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) gathers data on maternal attitudes and experiences before, during, and after pregnancy. This information is used to track progress toward improving maternal and infant health outcomes. States can use the CDC Levels of Care Assessment Tool (CDC LOCATeSM) in combination with other public health data to analyze how different levels of maternal and infant care impact health outcomes. For families experiencing the loss of an infant, grief resources are available through organizations such as First Candle, The Compassionate Friends, and March of Dimes. Additional resources include the CDC's National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities, Linked Birth and Infant Death Data from the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics, and information on drowning prevention and child passenger safety from the CDC's National Center for Injury Prevention and Control.
